summary: A BBN note on software checksumming added to the IMP and TIP programs to improve network reliability. The designers had first assumed only communication circuits were error-prone, then added checks for errors in other parts, and advise host staff to note two sections that may need changes in their procedures.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC describes software checks added to IMPs to detect errors caused by hardware and software failures. The checks also sent error information to the Network Control Center for diagnosis.

questions: why did arpanet add software checksums
what hardware errors did software checksums detect
how did arpanet protect routing messages
subtitle: How IMP software checksums were used to detect network and hardware errors.

tldr.problem: Experience showed that IMP memory, processors, and interfaces could corrupt packets and routing messages, not just communication circuits.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes software checksums on packets and routing information, with detected packet errors discarded and reported to the NCC.
tldr.outcome: The changes supported diagnosis and fault isolation; the author also describes limits and planned future checks.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 528's status as Unknown. The RFC describes reliability changes and future plans for IMP systems.

sections.title: Failures Beyond the Communication Circuits
sections.content:
The RFC says network operators had found errors that could not be explained only by communication circuit failures. IMP memory or interfaces could alter packet data or routing information, and a single bad routing message could disrupt network traffic.

The report describes software checksums as a way both to detect such errors and to provide information for remote diagnosis.
sections.plainLanguage: Errors could happen inside an IMP, not only on the circuit between IMPs. A bad routing message could affect traffic across the network.

sections.title: Checking Packets and Reporting Errors
sections.content:
The IMP program computes a software checksum for a packet and verifies it at each intermediate IMP and before delivery to the destination Host. If a received checksum is wrong, the packet is discarded; the previous IMP retransmits because it receives no acknowledgement.

The RFC says errors and a copy of the packet are reported to the Network Control Center. Its checksum is a simple sum of packet words plus the number of words, and the authors acknowledge that its error-detection capability is limited.
sections.plainLanguage: Each IMP checks a packet's checksum as the packet travels. If a check fails, the receiving IMP discards the packet and the previous IMP can retransmit it.

sections.title: Protecting Routing Information and Host Use
sections.content:
The routing program builds a checksum from the intended routing message contents and verifies it before transmission. The RFC also describes checksums of routing program code, with a request for a reload if a discrepancy is found.

Other sections discuss Host retransmission after incomplete transmission and recovery for long TIP magnetic-tape transfers. These changes are described as responses to failures and interruptions.
sections.plainLanguage: Routing messages and routing code also receive checks because errors there can affect the network. The RFC describes separate recovery changes for Host messages and tape transfers.

sections.title: Cost and Future Plans
sections.content:
The checksum calculation takes 2 milliseconds per word according to the RFC. On a 516 IMP, the reported effective processor bandwidth for full-length store-and-forward packets falls from a megabit per second to 875 kilobits per second.

The authors outline plans for a hardware CRC generator and possible checks between Hosts and IMPs. These are presented as future design plans.
sections.plainLanguage: Checksums use processing capacity, and the RFC gives a measured bandwidth reduction for a 516 IMP. It also describes hardware checks planned for a future IMP design.
